title: The Lesson I Learned From Bezalel
paragraphs:
The Lesson I Learned From Bezalel
The Man Nobody Expected God to Choose... and Why His Story Might Change Yours Forever
Most people think God only uses preachers.
Prophets.
Missionaries.
Evangelists.
People standing behind pulpits with microphones in their hands and crowds hanging on every word.
That is what many of us secretly believe.
We assume the closer someone appears to ministry, the closer they must be to God's heart.
But then Bezalel appears in Scripture.
And suddenly everything changes.
His story is not loud.
It is not flashy.
There are no recorded sermons.
No miracles.
No armies defeated.
No famous speeches.
Yet God did something so extraordinary with this man that his story still echoes thousands of years later.
And if you understand why, it might completely transform the way you see your purpose, your work, your gifts, and even your ordinary daily life.
Because Bezalel teaches us something most Christians desperately need to remember:
God is not only glorified through what happens in the church.
He is glorified through what happens in the hands of His people.

The first time we meet Bezalel, Israel is in the wilderness. The nation has witnessed miracles beyond imagination. They have watched the sea split apart. They have seen bread fall from heaven. They have heard the voice of God thunder from Sinai.
And yet when God begins establishing the Tabernacle—the place where His presence would dwell among His people—He does something unexpected.
Instead of calling another prophet...
He calls an artist.
Exodus 31:2-5 says:

"See, I have called by name Bezalel the son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, and I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with ability and intelligence, with knowledge and all craftsmanship, to devise artistic designs, to work in gold, silver, and bronze, in cutting stones for setting, and in carving wood, to work in every craft."
The Hebrew text uses a remarkable phrase:
וָאֲמַלֵּא אֹתוֹ רוּחַ אֱלֹהִים
Va'amalle oto Ruach Elohim
"I have filled him with the Spirit of God."
Think about that.
The first person in Scripture explicitly described as being filled with the Spirit of God was not a preacher.
Not a king.
Not a warrior.
An artisan.
A craftsman.
A creator.
A builder.
A man whose worship looked like skilled work.
Many believers spend years wondering if what they do matters to God.
The teacher wonders.
The carpenter wonders.
The business owner wonders.
The writer wonders.
The artist wonders.
The mechanic wonders.
The mother wonders.
The employee sitting in a cubicle wonders.
"Does God care about what I do?"
Bezalel answers with a resounding yes.
His life shatters the false divide between sacred and ordinary.
The world often asks, "How much money can you make?"
God asks, "How much glory can you bring Me?"
Those are very different questions.
Bezalel's calling reminds us that excellence can be an act of worship.
Integrity can be an act of worship.
Creativity can be an act of worship.
Building can be an act of worship.
Serving can be an act of worship.
Working can be an act of worship.
When done for the glory of God, ordinary things become holy things.
The Apostle Paul would later write:
The Greek phrase is:
πάντα εἰς δόξαν Θεοῦ ποιεῖτε
panta eis doxan Theou poieite
"Do everything for the glory of God."
Not some things.
Not church things.
Everything.
This is where Bezalel's story becomes deeply personal.
Because many people secretly believe God could never use them.
They see their failures.
Their weaknesses.
Their past.
Their mistakes.
Their scandals.
And they conclude that God must have chosen someone else.
But the Gospel tells a different story.
The Bible is filled with people who were broken before they were useful.
Moses was a fugitive.
David was an adulterer.
Peter was a denier.
Paul was a persecutor.
Yet God rewrote their stories through grace.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
That is the beauty of Jesus Christ.
He specializes in rewriting what sin tried to destroy.
The world remembers your worst moment.
Jesus offers a new beginning.
The world labels you by your failures.
Jesus calls you by your future.
The world sees scandal.
Jesus sees redemption.
The world sees ruins.
Jesus sees restoration.
This is why Bezalel's story matters.
Because his life is not merely about craftsmanship.
It is about calling.
And calling is never about making much of ourselves.
It is about making much of Christ.
Every skill you possess.
Every gift you have been given.
Every opportunity placed before you.
Every resource entrusted to you.
All of it ultimately belongs to Him.
Psalm 24:1 reminds us:
"לַיהוָה הָאָרֶץ וּמְלוֹאָהּ"
LaYHWH ha'aretz u'melo'ah
"The earth is the LORD's and everything in it."
Everything.
Including your talents.
Including your story.
Including your future.
And perhaps that is the lesson I learned from Bezalel.
God does not measure significance the way we do.
He is not impressed by fame.
He is not impressed by followers.
He is not impressed by influence.
He is impressed by faithfulness.
The person quietly serving Christ with excellence may be accomplishing more for eternity than someone standing in front of millions.
Because God sees what people overlook.
And He rewards what the world ignores.
Maybe you feel unseen right now.
Maybe your work feels small.
Maybe your efforts feel forgotten.
Maybe nobody applauds what you do.
Maybe nobody notices the sacrifices.
Maybe nobody understands the battles you fight.
But God sees.
The same God who called Bezalel by name knows your name too.
The same God who filled Bezalel with His Spirit still empowers His people today.
The same God who transformed fishermen into apostles and persecutors into missionaries can transform your life through Jesus Christ.
Do not underestimate what God can do with a surrendered heart.
History repeatedly proves that ordinary people become extraordinary when placed in the hands of an extraordinary Savior.
And perhaps while reading this, you realized something.
The greatest masterpiece Bezalel ever worked on was not the Tabernacle.
The greatest masterpiece God is working on is you.
Scripture says in Ephesians 2:10:
"For we are His workmanship."
The Greek word is ποίημα (poiēma).
It is where we get the word "poem."
You are God's workmanship.
His masterpiece.
His ongoing work of grace.
And if your story feels broken right now, remember this:
Jesus is still writing.
Be honest.
This may have touched something deeper than you expected.
Someone you know may be carrying a burden they have never spoken about, and this message may be the reminder they need today.
Every share extends the reach of the Gospel beyond what we could accomplish alone.
The God who filled Bezalel with His Spirit is still writing masterpieces from lives the world nearly discarded.
